articles.title: Keplr Web3Auth Breach: Social Login Keys Exposed
articles.excerpt: Originally published at Keplr Web3Auth Breach: Social Login Keys Exposed. On 6–7 November 2026, Keplr paused Google and Apple login after users reported unauthorized transactions on accounts created t…
articles.body: Originally published at Keplr Web3Auth Breach: Social Login Keys Exposed . On 6–7 November 2026 , Keplr paused Google and Apple login after users reported unauthorized transactions on accounts created through those social sign-in paths. Web3Auth (the Consensys-owned provider behind those embedded wallets, also branded as MetaMask Embedded Wallets) then said it had identified a security issue in its infrastructure affecting certain embedded wallets used by Keplr , leading to a private key breach for some social-login accounts. This is not a consensus bug and not a Keplr smart-contract exploit. It is an off-chain custody dependency failure: wallets that never showed users a recovery phrase still held spendable keys behind a third-party service.

articles.body: Square graph paper is two for loops. Isometric and hexagon paper look almost as simple, and my first version of each was wrong in a way that only showed up once I printed it. Here is what I ended up doing for a printable paper generator, with the bugs included. All coordinates are PDF points (1/72 inch), so a "side of 0.25 inch" is 18 pt. Isometric paper: three families of parallel lines Isometric paper is a tiling of equilateral triangles with side s . It's made of three sets of parallel lines: one vertical, and two at ±30° from the horizontal (or, the way I find easier to think about, lines whose normals point at 0°, 60° and 120°). Within each family the lines are s·√3/2 apart. That's the height of a triangle, not its side.

articles.title: Your Free Server Forgets Everything: Five Ephemeral-Deployment Myths and a State Probe
articles.excerpt: I keep reading the same three lines in deploy channels. "It worked yesterday." "The file was there." "The model knew my name." None of those are evidence of memory. They are evidence of a lucky restar…
articles.body: I keep reading the same three lines in deploy channels. "It worked yesterday." "The file was there." "The model knew my name." None of those are evidence of memory. They are evidence of a lucky restart window. Free compute and free model endpoints are usually shared and disposable. That is the deal. The trap is treating them as stateful by default. So here is a myth-busting FAQ, plus a probe you can run in five minutes. Myth 1: "The disk survives a restart" Sometimes it does. Sometimes you land on the same machine by chance. Your test is confirming nothing. Start with a repeatable probe. It writes one small JSON file, prints the previous contents, and exits. # state_probe.py — stdlib only, safe to run anywhere import json , os , socket , time , uuid STATE = os . environ .

articles.body: From Cricket Bans to Binding Pockets: Building Mental Models for Viral Glycoproteins in VR The notification hit my phone at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. EU bans house cricket protein in food products — EFSA cites insufficient safety data on allergen cross-reactivity. I stared at the screen, thumb hovering. Three years of grant proposals, late-night sequencing runs, and that one spectacular failure with the cryo-EM grid — all circling back to a regulatory footnote about insects I'd never even held. My lab works on viral glycoproteins. Not crickets. But the EFSA panel's reasoning — "structural homology between invertebrate tropomyosin and cricket allergens cannot be excluded" — used the exact language I'd written in Aim 2 of my last R01. Structural homology.

articles.title: A Model May Propose a Documentation Example; Only a Human Can Assert What It Prints
articles.excerpt: The rule I apply is short: every fenced block in a documentation file is either executed by CI or labeled illustrative with a named owner. The model may propose the code in either case, but only a hum…
articles.body: The rule I apply is short: every fenced block in a documentation file is either executed by CI or labeled illustrative with a named owner. The model may propose the code in either case, but only a human may assert what that code prints. That single constraint removes the most common defect in model-drafted docs, which is a confident example that has never run. This is a narrower claim than "generate your documentation", and it is deliberately narrower, because the artifact below fits on one screen and blocks a whole class of review arguments. The executor is plain Python with no dependencies, and the gate treats an unlabeled fence as a policy violation rather than a style nit. 1.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.

articles.body: We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034.

articles.title: 'I think we will prevail': NASA chief Jared Isaacman on Artemis, China and the new moon race (exclusive)
articles.excerpt: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during a a Dec. 3, 2025 confirmation hearing. In October of 2026, Isaacman sat down with Space.com to discuss the future of the space agency.
articles.body: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition. "I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com. We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program , and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
